overview: My capstone, Imisoro AI, is a bilingual (Kinyarwanda/English) RAG assistant that helps Rwandan small businesses understand and meet their RRA tax obligations. It includes rule-based tax calculators and a personalised deadline calendar with SMS/email reminders. Reminders and education only help if they arrive at the right time without overwhelming the owner, so this assignment learns the assistant's engagement policy. I built a custom Gymnasium environment that simulates one tax year of a small business. In it, a coaching agent chooses each week between waiting, reminding, running the calculator, teaching, nudging records or savings, and escalating to RRA. Four TorchRL agents (DQN, REINFORCE, PPO, A2C) were trained on the same environment with the same 300,000-step budget, each with 12 hyperparameter configurations (48 runs plus 8 seed-robustness runs). They were evaluated greedily on 200 unseen businesses and on a harder, unseen 'stress' population. PPO performed best (mean return −6.2, 74.8% of returns filed on time, versus 36.6% with no coaching). Every agent, however, over-contacts fragile owners in the stress population, which is the main limitation reported.
agent: The agent is the Imisoro AI engagement policy acting for one business owner. Each step is one week. The agent sees the obligation calendar, the business profile and app-side engagement signals, but not the owner's true knowledge, trust or fatigue. It acts through the channels the product actually has (SMS, email, in-app calculator, lessons, nudges) plus a limited human escalation to RRA. Its capabilities are bounded: an intervention only takes effect if the owner responds, with probability (0.3 + 0.7·trust)·(1 − fatigue)·channel affinity. Email affinity equals the owner's digital literacy.
why_rl: Actions change persistent state that matters weeks later. Lessons raise knowledge, which makes every future filing more likely. Savings and records nudges must happen before a deadline to pay off. Each contact adds fatigue that persists, and too much contact makes the owner opt out of the product. Rewards are delayed (mostly at deadlines, up to 13 weeks apart) and depend on the whole sequence of decisions, not on any single prediction. A per-week classifier that predicts 'will this owner miss the deadline?' cannot weigh teaching now against reminding later, or contacting now against keeping the owner engaged for the rest of the year. That is a sequential credit-assignment problem, which is what RL solves.
reward: Rewards follow the mission (on-time compliance at low burden to the owner). An obligation filed and fully paid on time gives +10. One filed on time but underpaid (set-aside cash < 60% of the liability) gives +4, reflecting interest on the unpaid balance. A missed deadline gives −15, reflecting RRA penalties and lost trust. Each intervention has a small cost (SMS −0.1, email −0.05, calculator/records −0.2, lesson −0.3, savings −0.1) that stands in for message cost and owner time. RRA escalation costs −2 because staff time is scarce, and escalating with no quota left adds a further −1. An owner who opts out ends the episode with −25. At year end the agent receives 5 × final knowledge, rewarding capability that outlasts the year.
p_on_time: At each deadline, P(on time) = clip(0.10 + 0.45·prep + 0.25·knowledge + 0.12·salience + 0.15·records, 0, 0.98). Preparation grows with calculator use and escalation, and naturally by 0.25·knowledge per week in the last three weeks. Salience comes from an SMS in the deadline week or the week before. SMS reminders sent more than three weeks before a deadline lower trust by 0.05 (perceived as spam).
start_terminal: Start state: at reset a business profile is sampled. The regime is flat (35%), lump-sum (35%) or real (30%); real-regime firms are VAT-registered with probability 0.9; employees occur with probability 0.4 (+0.3 for the real regime). The profile defines the RRA calendar: VAT and PAYE monthly on the 15th; flat/lump-sum quarterly on 15 Jan/Apr/Jul/Oct; real regime annual return on 31 March plus prepayments on 30 June, 30 September and 31 December. The resulting load ranges from 4 to 28 deadlines a year. Latent state is drawn from knowledge U(0.1, 0.5), trust U(0.4, 0.8), records U(0.1, 0.5), cash U(0, 0.3), with fatigue 0. Terminal conditions: (i) termination when the owner opts out (fatigue > 0.45 triggers opt-out with probability 3·(fatigue − 0.45) per week; fatigue decays ×0.75 weekly); (ii) truncation at week 52 (year end). The stress scenario (evaluation only) samples lower knowledge (0–0.25), trust (0.25–0.55), records and literacy, more employers, and fatigue that builds 1.4× faster.
visual: The renderer (environment/rendering.py) is a Three.js 3D scene served by a lightweight Python HTTP server. After every step the environment pushes a JSON snapshot to GET /state, and the page animates it. Interventions fly as coloured orbs from the Imisoro tower to the shop, and escalations travel to the RRA office. Calendar pillars turn green or red when deadlines resolve, and the owner's six latent variables appear as 3D bars and HUD gauges. The terminal prints a verbose line per week (action, response, reward, return, state, events).
dqn_design: Network: MLP 21 → 128 → 128 → 8 (ReLU) estimating Q(s, a) over the 8 actions, wrapped in TorchRL's QValueActor. Exploration uses EGreedyModule with linear ε annealing. Transitions from the TorchRL Collector (64 steps per batch) go into a TensorDictReplayBuffer (LazyTensorStorage), and after 2,000 random warm-up steps the agent performs several gradient updates per batch. The loss is DQNLoss with smooth-L1 TD error, double-DQN action selection and a delayed target network updated softly (τ) or hard (every N updates). Adam is used with gradient clipping at 10. The greedy policy is argmax Q.
pg_design: All three methods share the same actor: MLP 21 → 64 → 64 → 8 (tanh) producing logits for a OneHotCategorical distribution (TorchRL ProbabilisticActor), plus a separate value MLP (ValueOperator) of the same size. Data comes from 8 parallel environments (SerialEnv) through the TorchRL Collector. REINFORCE collects complete episodes, computes discounted Monte-Carlo returns and optimises ReinforceLoss with an optional baseline (learned value, batch mean or none), return normalisation and an entropy bonus. PPO uses GAE advantages and ClipPPOLoss over several epochs of shuffled minibatches per rollout. A2C uses GAE/n-step advantages and A2CLoss with a single synchronous update per short rollout. At evaluation, all policies act greedily (argmax logits).
fairness: Every run uses the identical environment class, observation and action spaces, reward function and a budget of 300,000 environment steps (about 5,750 simulated tax years). Evaluation uses the same 200 held-out seeds (never seen in training) for every model, plus 200 businesses from the stress population. Each algorithm's best configuration was retrained with two extra seeds.
impl_intro: Each table lists 12 configurations; run 1 is the default and every other run changes one or two controls. 'Mean reward' is the greedy evaluation return on 200 unseen businesses (on-time % alongside). The highlighted row is the best configuration. Full per-run logs are in logs/, and every model is saved in models/.
dqn_analysis: The target-network schedule mattered most. A hard copy every 200 updates (run 8) gave the best return (−19.8), while copying every 2,000 (run 9) slowed value propagation (−30.7). Turning off double DQN (run 10) dropped compliance to 58.8%: overestimated Q-values favoured cheap records/savings nudges. γ = 0.995 (run 5) made Q-estimates diverge (mean max-Q above 700, Fig. 3) and returns fell to −53.6. γ = 0.9 trained stably but became myopic and generalised worst to stress owners (−102.9). Fast ε decay (run 6: 10% of training, ε_end 0.01) locked in a poor policy early (−48.9). A small, recent replay buffer (run 11) gave the best stress return (−49.2) and compliance (71.8%), which suggests stale transitions hurt as the policy changes.
reinforce_analysis: REINFORCE was the noisiest learner (late-training reward sd 15.9, versus 8.6 for PPO). A learned value baseline (run 1, −18.3) beat a batch-mean baseline (run 3, −26.0); with no baseline (run 2) returns were similar but compliance fell to 61.4%. A low learning rate (run 4, 3e-4) collapsed to a deterministic 'always teach' policy: 70.8% on-time in training, but only 25.6% on stress owners. γ = 0.9 (run 6) could not credit rewards that arrive weeks later (−48.8). Larger batches of 16 episodes (run 8) reduced gradient variance and gave the highest compliance (73.5%). The wider network (run 11) had the best mean return (−16.6) but the largest spread (±55.2).
ppo_analysis: PPO had the best and most consistent results: 9 of 12 runs scored above −30. More optimisation per rollout helped: 10 epochs (run 6) reached −6.2 and 74.8% on-time, while 2 epochs with large minibatches (run 7) reached only −20.5. A low learning rate (1e-4, run 2) learned too slowly (−51.2), and 1e-3 (run 3) was unstable (±77.9). Clip ε of 0.1–0.3 made little difference (−13.5 to −16.0). A short-horizon advantage (GAE λ = 0.8, run 8) badly hurt credit assignment for deadline rewards (−41.4), and γ = 0.995 (run 9) gave the highest compliance (76.1%). With no entropy bonus (run 10) entropy collapsed early (Fig. 4) and the policy got stuck on records/savings nudges (−28.7). With 0.05 (run 11) entropy stayed near 1.85 nats, so the policy remained too random to time reminders well.
a2c_analysis: A2C was the most sensitive to rollout length. The default 8-step rollout reached −48.1. Five steps was worse, while 32 steps per environment (run 5) jumped to −20.6 with the highest compliance of all agents (75.9%). A 32-week bootstrap horizon covers the 4–13-week gaps between deadlines. γ = 0.9 was the worst run (−67.9): the policy waited 55% of weeks because deadline rewards were discounted away. The learning rate needed to be high enough (2e-3: −33.4 vs 2.5e-4: −56.3, which collapsed to SMS/email only). Adding advantage normalisation with a larger critic weight destabilised learning (−58.6). Most A2C runs dipped to about −80 in the first 50k steps before recovering (Fig. 5), showing the instability of single-step updates on small batches.
cumulative: Every learned policy beats the rule-based references by a wide margin (Section 5a table, Fig. 6). PPO reaches the highest final return and keeps improving steadily after about 100k steps. REINFORCE ends close to PPO in training reward (−9.1 over the last 10% of training) but is far noisier, and its greedy evaluation return is lower (−16.6). DQN improves quickly to about −25 by 100k steps and then plateaus with oscillations. A2C improves slowly and steadily, finishing at −15.7. Over three seeds PPO's advantage holds (−4.5 ± 5.7 vs −21.3 to −27.9 for the others). The DQN and A2C best runs regress over extra seeds (−19.8 → −27.9 and −20.6 → −27.0), because choosing the best of 12 runs on one seed is optimistically biased.
baselines: Rule-based references on the same 200 businesses: no contact −111.7 (36.6% on time); random actions −57.2 (65.9%); and a deadline heuristic (savings nudge 3 weeks before, calculator 2 weeks before, SMS 1 week before) −78.8 (52.4%). The heuristic does worse than random because it never teaches and never improves records, which shows that the long-term actions matter.
stability: DQN: the TD loss rises from about 1.8 to 3–3.5 as the agent learns, which is expected because the value scale grows as returns improve. The mean max-Q stabilises around 40 for the best and default runs, and only γ = 0.995 diverges (Fig. 3). The ε schedule reaches its floor at 90k steps, after which DQN's reward mostly oscillates rather than improves. Policy-gradient methods (Fig. 4): PPO lowers its entropy smoothly from ln 8 = 2.08 to about 1.16 nats, the clearest sign of a converging policy. REINFORCE's entropy jumps back up repeatedly (e.g. to 1.9 at 175k steps), matching its noisy reward curve. A2C sits in between at about 1.4–1.6. The PPO entropy-coefficient comparison shows the expected ordering (0.05 keeps the policy most stochastic) and explains why 0.01 was the best trade-off.
convergence: Using the smoothed training curve of each best run: PPO first reaches −20 after about 86k steps (about 1,650 episodes) and −12 after 121k steps (about 2,300). DQN reaches −30 fastest (79k steps, about 1,500 episodes) but needs 227k steps to touch −20 and does not hold it. REINFORCE crosses −30 earliest (47k steps) because of high-variance spikes, reaching −20 only at 191k and −12 at 264k. A2C is slowest (−30 at 172k, −20 at 209k). Across all 12 configurations (Fig. 5) PPO's runs are tightly grouped and most are still improving at 300k. DQN's runs plateau early, REINFORCE's are very jagged, and A2C's runs differ mainly by rollout length.
generalization: On unseen businesses from the training distribution, all agents generalise (no opt-outs, 65–76% on time). The stress population is harder: owners know less, trust less and tire 1.4× faster. There, on-time filing falls to 45–59%, and every agent causes many opt-outs: DQN 74%, REINFORCE 61%, PPO 84%, A2C 99.5%. The contact rhythm learned on typical owners is too intense for fragile ones. Stress returns (−42 to −62) still beat all baselines, but they partly overstate performance: an opt-out ends the episode, so later missed-deadline penalties are never counted. A2C's best policy teaches 77% of weeks (Fig. 7). That works on typical owners but is the most fatiguing pattern and fails worst under stress. The DQN run with a small replay buffer and PPO with 10 epochs kept the best balance of compliance and robustness.
behaviour: The learned policies are interpretable. Over the 200 evaluation years, PPO (the deployed agent) behaves like a sensible coach. It sends SMS reminders almost only when a deadline is due this week (87% of such weeks) or next week (54%). It uses savings nudges when the next deadline is 4–8 weeks away (39–59%), so money is set aside in time. It front-loads investment: lessons take 39% of weeks in the first quarter and fall to 1% by the second half of the year, and all RRA escalations are used in the first quarter, when owners' knowledge is lowest. It waits more as the year goes on (3% → 15% of weeks) to let fatigue recover, and it never uses email, which reaches only digitally literate owners. In the default replay used for the video (seed 2026), the second business (flat regime with employees, 16 deadlines) ends the year with 14 of 16 returns filed on time (+83.2). The first business, which starts with low knowledge (0.30) and trust, files only 2 of 4 on time: a reminder that the agent cannot overcome an owner who ignores most contacts.
conclusion: PPO is the best method for this environment: it has the highest evaluation return (−6.2; −4.5 ± 5.7 over three seeds), high compliance (74.8% vs 36.6% without coaching) and the smoothest convergence. Its clipped multi-epoch updates make good use of each rollout and stay stable even though rewards are sparse and delayed. A2C matched PPO's compliance only with long 32-step rollouts and was the most fragile under distribution shift. REINFORCE found good policies but with high variance between updates and between seeds. Value-based DQN learned fastest at first but plateaued, because ε-greedy exploration and bootstrapped targets struggle when rewards are rare and actions have long-delayed effects. Its stability depended heavily on the target-update schedule and double-Q correction.
limitations: The owner dynamics are a hand-designed simulator, not fitted to data. The calendar simplifies RRA rules, and the behavioural coefficients are assumptions to be calibrated with the capstone survey and pilot logs. Each configuration used one seed, with three seeds only for each algorithm's best configuration, so small differences between runs are not significant. All agents fail under higher fatigue sensitivity, and the opt-out penalty (−25) is smaller than the penalties an owner who stays and misses deadlines can accumulate. A reward redesign (for example, charging the expected penalties for the rest of the year on opt-out), or domain randomisation of fatigue during training, is needed before real use.
integration: Each trained policy is serialised three ways: as a PyTorch state_dict (.pt), as a TorchScript module (.ts), and as JSON metadata with its config and evaluation results. The command uv run main.py serve exposes POST /api/recommend, which takes the 21-feature observation and returns the recommended action and its scores. The Imisoro web/mobile backend can call this endpoint weekly per user, and the existing calculator and calendar services supply the observation features (Section 2c).
future: Calibrate the simulator with survey and pilot data; train with randomised fatigue sensitivity and a monthly contact limit; use a recurrent (LSTM) policy to infer fatigue from engagement history; and evaluate offline on logged reminders before any live A/B test with RRA.
